title_original: 《女籃巨人烏莉亞》：競技之外的暈眩與其他
title_zh: 《女籃巨人烏莉亞》：競技之外的暈眩與其他
summary_zh: 来源摘录：在故事的大多階段，我們接收到的重心首先是普世問題：關於一個人物，之於她所身處環境的格格不入，但在故事之外，演員的性別身分與詮釋，仍在許多時刻出現（無關乎在或不在電影預設之內）關於性別的觀看效果。我們要如何理解眼前所見的，遭遇特定身體處境的人物，她的性別與「性」為何，她的社會互動與身體，存在什麼特徵？ 這篇文章 《女籃巨人烏莉亞》：競技之外的暈眩與其他 最早出現於 釀電影 。

在劇場，由男性演員演出女性角色，有較明確的傳統可供依循，而他嘗試在電影裡實現這個構想，且是面對一個在當地幾近家喻戶曉的真實人物，並非採用象徵手法，而以嚴肅且接近寫實的背景設計來詮釋她。 無可避免地，這個決策會為電影增加話題與爭議性，尤其關於女性身分的代表性問題。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "若單純以作品呈現來看，一個由現實 30 歲上下的成年男性所詮釋的 16 歲青少女，Karlis Arnolds Avots 並未主張自己在生理或性別認同上跨越這些界線，而更多是嘗試以普世性的情感，去看待這名角色身處的困難。 《女籃巨人烏莉亞》最主要被突顯的人物特色，是烏莉亞對身體的不安，高大且壯碩的骨架讓她成為球探的目標，卻也因此與社群環境產生疏離感。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在角色的描繪上，Karlis Arnolds Avots 加強揣摩這種無法融入群體的肢體特徵，烏莉亞的形象顯得害羞或侷促，而她在球場上的反應有時看起來笨拙且不自信，而這些不自信並非是以技巧、天賦成長的成敗所衡量，更在於故事對她心理狀態的側重：她對她的身體保有疑惑。 在故事呈現中，這種疑惑的重心不完全關於性別，但因為觀眾注視著一個成年男性的、非依靠象徵處理的表演，這種不安便有了多重的理解空間和聯想。"}, {"type": "烏莉亞所體會的，不僅只是一般青春故事的內心疏離，她與他人無法融入的困惑，多方向地在宗教、族群、經濟狀況與體格等現實狀況上感到不安。我們看到一個青少女倍受煎熬，電影中亦提及球員身分的荷爾蒙檢測，或是表現警員以檢查生殖器的粗暴做法臨檢其性別身分，然而這些情節並未出現明確的現實落點，許多時候，它們僅是呼應著作為故事背景的蘇聯社會與時代氛圍。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在故事的大多階段，我們接收到的重心首先是普世問題：關於一個人物，之於她所身處環境的格格不入，但在故事之外，演員的性別身分與詮釋，仍在許多時刻出現（無關乎在或不在電影預設之內）關於性別的觀看效果。 我們要如何理解眼前所見的，遭遇特定身體處境的人物，她的性別與「性」為何，她的社會互動與身體，存在什麼特徵？又，為何這些特徵是重要的，真實的烏莉亞對身體的不安是否能與之類比？而再一次，這個類比能否建立，本身又是重要的嗎？這些問題據此往下綿延，並不容易在作品本身獲得解答。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在關於性別的判斷之外，導演凱里斯與曾獲柏林影展銀熊獎肯定的攝影指導沃傑赫・斯大隆（Wojciech Staron），共同在電影形式上加強了烏莉亞內外掙扎的角色狀態。電影以 4：3 的景框、黑白攝影呈現，準確且節制。 形式嚴密地控制故事訊息，位處在景框內的人物時常是模糊的，或處在焦距之外；極端且高亮度的光線、遮掩的門框或牆板，或單純因為身處於主觀之中，而無法得見全觀的視覺印象。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "故事時常呼應烏莉亞當下的情緒判斷，觀眾大多時候都在僅有部分可見的位置中經驗故事，而透過與旁人的對比，我們會反覆看到烏莉亞高大的身形，在構圖中反覆顯得突兀而難以親近。 當她離家、與同儕沐浴，或單純在球場上感到暈眩，這些情緒並非直接透過烏莉亞的視線為主觀鏡頭的呈現，但仍改變觀眾觀看到故事的方式。"}, {"type": "image", "對於角色內心狀態的視覺刻劃，並不完全透過表演或情節對白來傳達。這是本片從一般的競技運動敘事中轉向的方式，比起運動本身的輸或贏，甚至是這些輸贏如何影響身處在運動中的人物，《女籃巨人烏莉亞》關心的似乎更是一個，在運動上顯現天賦、突出於常人的人，在一個並不穩定的環境裡，更可能處於何種生活狀態。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "烏莉亞同時身處在她的青春期，在與同儕並不相容的語言與宗教，在一個評判她身體價值的競技系統，也在六〇年代蘇聯的政治氛圍之中。 電影並未以任何一者決斷她的掙扎，角色關鍵的動作或選擇時常保持留白，我們不常見到巨大的情緒性爭執。這個做法保全了這部電影冷靜且專注的敘事策略，但偶爾讓人懷疑，我們是否是在一個虛構的人物故事當中，試圖尋得移情理解，而非真實地觀測一個具體發生過的事件。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "烏莉亞大多時候都身處邊緣，與自己的欲望共處。故事在一個複雜的社會背景中，處理著相對單純的青春期困惑，對群體歸屬或是親密關係的朦朧欲望。 這些欲望是電影主要的情緒來源，而在故事的尾段，匱乏的人際連結、對親密關係的想像，連結到她身為明日之星的競技「價值」，則對她產生另一次衝擊。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "劇本在此處活用了這個明確的戲劇化場景，表現教練與隊友們，對於烏莉亞在電影中段已有前例的不知所蹤感到不安，而最後她卻自行度過這個困境。 隨之而來的答案是，在這些波折發生時，她已經跟她的天賦建立了更緊密的精神連結，這個連結如今足以保護她。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "「籃球」在此處因此扮演著有趣的角色，不在球場上，而在球場下。這是許多競技運動電影偶爾會提出，但不常被視為主軸的觀點。超過競技現場的五感，或反覆自我拷問的技藝、勝負、功利磨練過程，運動在此回歸為個人精神方面的避風港。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "自然而然地，它關於「你的個人天賦（特質），與隨之而來的努力，會在某個時刻拯救你」，但它發生作用的時間點，並不在眾人從旁看到的一刻，甚至不盡然是電影選擇呈現給觀眾看到的一刻。 《女籃巨人烏莉亞》在此處選擇一條更單純的角度，去觀看人物的故事，有時候我們稱其為平靜，而在平靜之外的事情，都發生在故事之外。"}, {"type": "image", "url": 高雄電影節，以獨樹一格的選片視角與具爆發力的影像能量，持續撞擊當代觀影體驗的既定邊界。《釀電影》編輯室以「熱天午後」為策展專題，延伸自希臘導演康斯坦蒂娜．柯薩瑪尼（Konstantina Kotzamani）的短片代表作《雅典熱天午後》（Washingtonia，2014），連結柯薩瑪尼系列作品的城市、荒塚與冷酷異境。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本次專題將由獨立評論人黃曦與導演康斯坦蒂娜．柯薩瑪尼（Konstantina Kotzamani）進行深度訪談，藉由系譜性地閱讀柯薩瑪尼，觀眾方能照見導演從植物、自然科學與傳頌百年的神話中，刺向當代社會的體制、階級、語言等困境，由此提出一道粉嫩且霓虹的提問；與此同時，本專題亦同步收錄獨立評論人沈怡昕於坎城影展現場，與柯薩瑪尼圍繞新作《人魚戀習曲》（Titanic Ocean，2026）之對答集。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在本屆的「非典型視窗」單元片單，則集結 11 部來自世界各地的當代作品，此次專題將分別聚焦四部作品進行評論分析。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "其中包括，獨立評論人許騰云剖析曾以《愛情美樂地》（Joyland，2022）獲該屆坎城影展「一種注目單元」評審團大獎的巴基斯坦導演沙馬．蘇丹．庫薩特（Sarmad Sultan Khoosat），透過同為古典寓言的新作《新婚美樂地》（Lali），呈示喧騰、荒唐的禮讚與喪鐘，以及傳統婚姻制度下的女性宿命。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "曾任多年記者，現為文字工作者的阿潑（島嶼無風帶）帶領讀者走進韓國名導鄭智泳（정지영）新作《我的名字是⋯》（My Name），嘗試穿梭於當代校園、近代歷史之間，回顧被巨大歷史洪流所掩埋的「濟州四・三事件」（제주 4・3 사건）。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "獨立評論人蔡曉松則著眼改編自女籃球星烏莉安娜．謝米諾娃（Uļjana Semjonova）真實故事、拉脫維亞導演維斯圖爾．凱里斯（Viesturs Kairišs）於新作《女籃巨人烏莉亞》（Ulya）呈現的特異、詩意的鏡頭與表演呈現。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最後，由獨立評論人桑妮執筆法國邪典導演貝特朗．曼迪科（Bertrand Mandico）新作《羅馬瘋情畫》，探究一代名導如何攜手奧斯卡影后瑪莉詠．柯蒂亞（Marion 撰文／蔡曉松 劇照提供／高雄電影節 責任編輯／黃曦 核稿編輯／黃曦

2026 高雄電影節「非典型視窗」單元 ，拉脫維亞導演維斯圖爾・凱里斯（Viestur Kairish）新作《女籃巨人烏莉亞》（Ulya）入選今年坎城影展「一種注目」單元，電影的時間背景設定在 1964 年，描述拉脫維亞籃球傳奇人物烏莉安娜・謝米諾娃（Uļjana Semjonova，1952－2026）生涯早期的生活。

電影並非以一段特定的成就或競賽經驗著手，而著重在烏莉亞接觸籃球的早期背景：出身於傳統的俄羅斯舊禮儀派農民家庭，宗教、族群與蘇聯六〇年代的政治氛圍縈繞在電影敘事中，青少女離開貧窮的生長環境，進入一個能夠改變她生涯的教育與職業環境。

在傳記故事的色彩中，這些改變都被已經寫定的現實所許諾，必定會發生；儘管有著明確可操作的戲劇化成長故事基調，但《女籃巨人烏莉亞》並不將重心放在她的成就，它更多是一個身處自我懷疑的階段，對生活（而非競賽）充滿挫敗感的青少年敘事。

《女籃巨人烏莉亞》電影劇照／劇照提供：高雄電影節

電影的共同編劇之一，同時是演出烏莉亞（Ulya）的主要演員 Karlis Arnolds Avots，在作品成形的過程中扮演重要的位置。自承深受烏莉亞所影響，《女籃巨人烏莉亞》的劇本發想由 Karlis Arnolds Avots 本人開始，且最早就設定為由他親自主演的作品。

Karlis Arnolds Avots 原先是劇場演員，他與導演凱里斯從劇場開始合作； 在劇場，由男性演員演出女性角色，有較明確的傳統可供依循，而他嘗試在電影裡實現這個構想，且是面對一個在當地幾近家喻戶曉的真實人物，並非採用象徵手法，而以嚴肅且接近寫實的背景設計來詮釋她。 無可避免地，這個決策會為電影增加話題與爭議性，尤其關於女性身分的代表性問題。

若單純以作品呈現來看，一個由現實 30 歲上下的成年男性所詮釋的 16 歲青少女，Karlis Arnolds Avots 並未主張自己在生理或性別認同上跨越這些界線，而更多是嘗試以普世性的情感，去看待這名角色身處的困難。 《女籃巨人烏莉亞》最主要被突顯的人物特色，是烏莉亞對身體的不安，高大且壯碩的骨架讓她成為球探的目標，卻也因此與社群環境產生疏離感。

在角色的描繪上，Karlis Arnolds Avots 加強揣摩這種無法融入群體的肢體特徵，烏莉亞的形象顯得害羞或侷促，而她在球場上的反應有時看起來笨拙且不自信，而這些不自信並非是以技巧、天賦成長的成敗所衡量，更在於故事對她心理狀態的側重：她對她的身體保有疑惑。 在故事呈現中，這種疑惑的重心不完全關於性別，但因為觀眾注視著一個成年男性的、非依靠象徵處理的表演，這種不安便有了多重的理解空間和聯想。

《女籃巨人烏莉亞》電影劇照／劇照提供：高雄電影節

《女籃巨人烏莉亞》電影劇照／劇照提供：高雄電影節

烏莉亞所體會的，不僅只是一般青春故事的內心疏離，她與他人無法融入的困惑，多方向地在宗教、族群、經濟狀況與體格等現實狀況上感到不安。我們看到一個青少女倍受煎熬，電影中亦提及球員身分的荷爾蒙檢測，或是表現警員以檢查生殖器的粗暴做法臨檢其性別身分，然而這些情節並未出現明確的現實落點，許多時候，它們僅是呼應著作為故事背景的蘇聯社會與時代氛圍。

在故事的大多階段，我們接收到的重心首先是普世問題：關於一個人物，之於她所身處環境的格格不入，但在故事之外，演員的性別身分與詮釋，仍在許多時刻出現（無關乎在或不在電影預設之內）關於性別的觀看效果。 我們要如何理解眼前所見的，遭遇特定身體處境的人物，她的性別與「性」為何，她的社會互動與身體，存在什麼特徵？又，為何這些特徵是重要的，真實的烏莉亞對身體的不安是否能與之類比？而再一次，這個類比能否建立，本身又是重要的嗎？這些問題據此往下綿延，並不容易在作品本身獲得解答。

在關於性別的判斷之外，導演凱里斯與曾獲柏林影展銀熊獎肯定的攝影指導沃傑赫・斯大隆（Wojciech Staron），共同在電影形式上加強了烏莉亞內外掙扎的角色狀態。電影以 4：3 的景框、黑白攝影呈現，準確且節制。 形式嚴密地控制故事訊息，位處在景框內的人物時常是模糊的，或處在焦距之外；極端且高亮度的光線、遮掩的門框或牆板，或單純因為身處於主觀之中，而無法得見全觀的視覺印象。

故事時常呼應烏莉亞當下的情緒判斷，觀眾大多時候都在僅有部分可見的位置中經驗故事，而透過與旁人的對比，我們會反覆看到烏莉亞高大的身形，在構圖中反覆顯得突兀而難以親近。 當她離家、與同儕沐浴，或單純在球場上感到暈眩，這些情緒並非直接透過烏莉亞的視線為主觀鏡頭的呈現，但仍改變觀眾觀看到故事的方式。

《女籃巨人烏莉亞》電影劇照／劇照提供：高雄電影節

《女籃巨人烏莉亞》電影劇照／劇照提供：高雄電影節

對於角色內心狀態的視覺刻劃，並不完全透過表演或情節對白來傳達。這是本片從一般的競技運動敘事中轉向的方式，比起運動本身的輸或贏，甚至是這些輸贏如何影響身處在運動中的人物，《女籃巨人烏莉亞》關心的似乎更是一個，在運動上顯現天賦、突出於常人的人，在一個並不穩定的環境裡，更可能處於何種生活狀態。

烏莉亞同時身處在她的青春期，在與同儕並不相容的語言與宗教，在一個評判她身體價值的競技系統，也在六〇年代蘇聯的政治氛圍之中。 電影並未以任何一者決斷她的掙扎，角色關鍵的動作或選擇時常保持留白，我們不常見到巨大的情緒性爭執。這個做法保全了這部電影冷靜且專注的敘事策略，但偶爾讓人懷疑，我們是否是在一個虛構的人物故事當中，試圖尋得移情理解，而非真實地觀測一個具體發生過的事件。

烏莉亞大多時候都身處邊緣，與自己的欲望共處。故事在一個複雜的社會背景中，處理著相對單純的青春期困惑，對群體歸屬或是親密關係的朦朧欲望。 這些欲望是電影主要的情緒來源，而在故事的尾段，匱乏的人際連結、對親密關係的想像，連結到她身為明日之星的競技「價值」，則對她產生另一次衝擊。

劇本在此處活用了這個明確的戲劇化場景，表現教練與隊友們，對於烏莉亞在電影中段已有前例的不知所蹤感到不安，而最後她卻自行度過這個困境。 隨之而來的答案是，在這些波折發生時，她已經跟她的天賦建立了更緊密的精神連結，這個連結如今足以保護她。

《女籃巨人烏莉亞》電影劇照／劇照提供：高雄電影節

《女籃巨人烏莉亞》電影劇照／劇照提供：高雄電影節

「籃球」在此處因此扮演著有趣的角色，不在球場上，而在球場下。這是許多競技運動電影偶爾會提出，但不常被視為主軸的觀點。超過競技現場的五感，或反覆自我拷問的技藝、勝負、功利磨練過程，運動在此回歸為個人精神方面的避風港。

自然而然地，它關於「你的個人天賦（特質），與隨之而來的努力，會在某個時刻拯救你」，但它發生作用的時間點，並不在眾人從旁看到的一刻，甚至不盡然是電影選擇呈現給觀眾看到的一刻。 《女籃巨人烏莉亞》在此處選擇一條更單純的角度，去觀看人物的故事，有時候我們稱其為平靜，而在平靜之外的事情，都發生在故事之外。

《釀電影》熱天午後——𝟤𝟢𝟤𝟨 高雄電影節專題／圖像提供：釀電影

將於 2026 年 10 月 09 日正式開展的 2026 高雄電影節，以獨樹一格的選片視角與具爆發力的影像能量，持續撞擊當代觀影體驗的既定邊界。《釀電影》編輯室以「熱天午後」為策展專題，延伸自希臘導演康斯坦蒂娜．柯薩瑪尼（Konstantina Kotzamani）的短片代表作《雅典熱天午後》（Washingtonia，2014），連結柯薩瑪尼系列作品的城市、荒塚與冷酷異境。

本次專題將由獨立評論人黃曦與導演康斯坦蒂娜．柯薩瑪尼（Konstantina Kotzamani）進行深度訪談，藉由系譜性地閱讀柯薩瑪尼，觀眾方能照見導演從植物、自然科學與傳頌百年的神話中，刺向當代社會的體制、階級、語言等困境，由此提出一道粉嫩且霓虹的提問；與此同時，本專題亦同步收錄獨立評論人沈怡昕於坎城影展現場，與柯薩瑪尼圍繞新作《人魚戀習曲》（Titanic Ocean，2026）之對答集。

在本屆的「非典型視窗」單元片單，則集結 11 部來自世界各地的當代作品，此次專題將分別聚焦四部作品進行評論分析。

其中包括，獨立評論人許騰云剖析曾以《愛情美樂地》（Joyland，2022）獲該屆坎城影展「一種注目單元」評審團大獎的巴基斯坦導演沙馬．蘇丹．庫薩特（Sarmad Sultan Khoosat），透過同為古典寓言的新作《新婚美樂地》（Lali），呈示喧騰、荒唐的禮讚與喪鐘，以及傳統婚姻制度下的女性宿命。

曾任多年記者，現為文字工作者的阿潑（島嶼無風帶）帶領讀者走進韓國名導鄭智泳（정지영）新作《我的名字是⋯》（My Name），嘗試穿梭於當代校園、近代歷史之間，回顧被巨大歷史洪流所掩埋的「濟州四・三事件」（제주 4・3 사건）。

獨立評論人蔡曉松則著眼改編自女籃球星烏莉安娜．謝米諾娃（Uļjana Semjonova）真實故事、拉脫維亞導演維斯圖爾．凱里斯（Viesturs Kairišs）於新作《女籃巨人烏莉亞》（Ulya）呈現的特異、詩意的鏡頭與表演呈現。

最後，由獨立評論人桑妮執筆法國邪典導演貝特朗．曼迪科（Bertrand Mandico）新作《羅馬瘋情畫》，探究一代名導如何攜手奧斯卡影后瑪莉詠．柯蒂亞（Marion Cotillard）與《燃燒女子的畫像》（Portrait de la jeune fille en feu，2019）諾耶米．梅蘭特（Noémie Merlant），在情色食人科幻狂想中，以鉛黃電影與費里尼式的怪誕拼貼，交出當代垃圾美學與女性主義謝幕的迷人花火。

此外，《釀電影》編輯室也將於影展期間走訪高雄電影節，進行其他短篇評論分析：「年度主題：抓馬人間」單元之《飛瀑怒潮》（Niagara，1953）、《夢魘人妻》（DreamQuil，2026）；「多倫多亞洲電影節精選」單元之《海草之家》（Seagrass，2023）、《世界上最ㄅㄧㄤˋ的國家》（The Greatest Country in the World，2019）；「抓馬跨世代單元：阿莫多瓦 vs 哈維爾雙人組」單元之《黑球》（The Black Ball，2026）；「大銀幕必看經典」單元之《深深腥紅 導演版》（Deep Crimson Director's Cut）；「耽美主義」單元之《青春抹世物語》（What We Saw）；「特別放映」單元之《1949》（Fatherland，2026）。

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tanzanian filmmaker Neema Ngelime’s “The Ones With the Tempered Flowers,” Palestinian director Fitnat Waked’s “On the Sea Road” and “Where Do I Belong?,” from Sudanese director Ibrahim “Snoopy” Ahmad, were among the big winners at this year’s Durban FilmMart , which wrapped with an award ceremony on Monday night.", "links": [{"text": "Durban FilmMart", "url": "https://variety.com/t/durban-filmmart/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ngelime’s directorial debut took home five awards, including the prize for best non-fiction film from South Africa’s National Film and Video Foundation and awards from DOK Leipzig, Sheffield Doc Fest and Visions du Réel. Tanzanian filmmaker Neema Ngelime’s “The Ones With the Tempered Flowers,” Palestinian director Fitnat Waked’s “On the Sea Road” and “Where Do I Belong?,” from Sudanese director Ibrahim “Snoopy” Ahmad, were among the big winners at this year’s Durban FilmMart , which wrapped with an award ceremony on Monday night.

Ngelime’s directorial debut took home five awards, including the prize for best non-fiction film from South Africa’s National Film and Video Foundation and awards from DOK Leipzig, Sheffield Doc Fest and Visions du Réel. The film tells the story of a woman studying her body’s relationship to self and society, and the political weight placed on women’s bodies in Tanzania, and challenging duty masked as love.

Related Stories

Japan IP Market to Return to Cannes in 2027 as Tokyo Partnership Continues

Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’

“Where Do I Belong?” is the latest from Ahmad, who co-directed last year’s Sundance-premiering documentary “Khartoum.” The winner of four prizes at the DFM forum, it follows the director as he decides to leave Nairobi and return to his family in the Sudanese capital, combining documentary footage and hand-drawn pencil animation to tell an intimate and unconventional road movie. Also taking four awards was “On the Sea Road,” the debut feature from Waked, a documentary about the friendship forged between two Palestinian women separated by borders.

Among other standout projects was “The Boy Who Spoke Static,” from Nigeria’s Agbajowo Collective, the filmmaking group behind the 2024 Toronto premiere “The Legend of the Vagabond Queen of Lagos,” which won three prizes, including the prize for best fiction film from South Africa’s NFVF.

The ceremony capped a rousing edition of the pitch and finance forum at the DFM, which kicked off its 17th edition with a celebration of DFM alumnus “Ben’Imana,” from first-time Rwandan filmmaker Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo, which won the Cámera d’Or in Cannes and became that country’s first ever submission in the Oscar category for best international feature film.

Durban FilmMart Institute director Magdalene Reddy praised the “dynamic array of filmmakers and industry leaders” taking part in this year’s event and stressed how “the talent showcased in this year’s program and film projects exemplifies the strength of African cinema.

“The Durban FilmMart Institute…remains committed to building the industry,” she said. “Thank you for participating with such passion and professionalism in all the programs presented over the last four days. Thank you for connecting, for telling your stories. And thank you for shifting the world with us.”

article_text:
Keanu Reeves is set to star in Maelstrom , a new Netflix action flick from Carry-On ‘s Jaume Collet-Serra, sources have confirmed to Deadline.

Reeves takes over the lead from Reacher ‘s Alan Ritchson, who exited the project for undisclosed reasons. Reps for Netflix declined to comment.

In Maelstrom , a Federal Marshal assigned to protect the fiancée of an arms dealer turned witness must defend her through one brutal night as a hurricane cuts off communication, strands them without reinforcements, and unleashes the dealer’s men on their safe house.

Related Stories

Reed Hastings On Netflix Shakeup, YouTube Rivalry And How Streamer Can Go Back To "Being Thrilling"

Ted Sarandos Shrugs Off U.S. Troubles To Mark Netflix's 10 Years In Korea

The current draft of the script is by Mark Bianculli; the first draft was by the late Gregory Fitzpatrick. This is one of those projects that has been working its way through the system for many years, having first been set up as a spec at Warner Bros. back in 1993.

Watch on Deadline

Jeff Robinov will produce alongside Tabitha Shick and Talking Pictures.

Coming off the fourth installment of his John Wick franchise, Reeves has been aggressively expanding his slate of late. Most recently, he entered talks to lead James Wan’s take on South Korean crime actioner The Gangster, The Cop, The Devil for Paramount, where he’s also set to reprise his voice role of Shadow in Sonic the Hedgehog 4 . As we first reported, Reeves recently set up an adaptation of the forthcoming Oliver Lowe novel Kill Current: A Jon Hendricks Thriller as another starring vehicle. That film will mark the first project produced under his new banner Two Dragonflies. His partners are The Arena and Zando.

Other upcoming projects for Reeves include the Warner Bros. sci-fi flick Shiver and The Entertainment System Is Down , from multiple Palme d’Or winner Ruben Östlund. Page Six Hollywood announced his Maelstrom casting.

À 20 ans seulement, ELLIE avance à contre-courant. Autrice et compositrice, la jeune niçoise à la présence charismatique s’éloigne du cadre académique et se met à composer depuis sa chambre d’adolescente, avec pour seuls compagnons GarageBand et son téléphone. Dans un monde en perpétuel mouvement, elle prend le temps et se démarque avec des singles comme « In the Breach » et « On My Own », écrits en anglais pour dompter sa nature réservée, puis son EP Invisible Things, dans lequel la chanteuse multi-instrumentiste fait cohabiter des élans de rock avec des piano-voix.

Pour son premier clip Here Down on Earth , produit par le studio Remembers, on retrouve l’idée de la “chambre-refuge” : elle nous fait entrer dans un rêve (ou serait-ce un cauchemar ?) de 3 minutes, mêlant cinématographie, archives et créations 3D. On passe d’un champ de blé, à une cabane faite de bois dont le toit est recouvert de pans de draps. Une silhouette se découpe sur le crépuscule, les ailes déployées : comme un retour à la danse, discipline qui a formé la chanteuse aux boucles brunes. Puis la cabane protéiforme émerge d’un brouillard blanc traversé de faisceaux de lumière, avant que les flammes ne l’engloutissent, dans un incendie qui rappelle celui du Sacrifice d’Andreï Tarkovski.

Dans le même temps, la Terre s’embrase, comme pour signifier que c’est notre maison au sens large qui est menacée. Le clip s’achève sur la cabane ressuscitée, et la voix d’ELLIE, profonde et enveloppante, semble nous dire qu’une lueur perce peut-être l’obscurité.

article_text:
“ Gondhal ,” the Marathi-language thriller India has put forward for the international feature Oscar at the 99th Academy Awards, has launched its global trailer as its awards push moves into a new phase.

The film is the first feature from writer-director Santosh Davakhar. It was chosen from a field of 33 films in contention for India’s submission.

The story plays out over a single night in rural Maharashtra, during a Gondhal, a folk ritual in which devotion is expressed through song, dance and theatrical storytelling. Ishita Deshmukh plays Suman, a young wife stuck in a suffocating marriage. She tries to take back control by playing on the fixation her lover Sarjerao (Nishad Bhoir) has developed for her. As her desires run up against codes of honor and custom, the night ends in tragedy.

Related Stories

Kishor Kadam, Yogesh Sohoni and Anuj Prabhu also star. Amalendu Chaudhary shot the film, which opens with an unbroken take lasting 25 minutes. Legendary composer Ilaiyaraaja wrote the music and background score.

“Global perceptions of Indian cinema are often shaped by narratives of poverty and caste conflict – important realities, but not the complete expression of India,” said Davakhar. “India is also a civilization of extraordinary cultural wealth, sustained by traditions, music, and collective memory. I created this film to bring one such powerful tradition to the global screen through a culturally authentic and universal cinematic language.”

Davakhar won the Silver Peacock for best director at the 56th International Film Festival of India (IFFI). Jury members at the festival called the film “like a Shakespearean fable set in a real world.”

Davakhar produced the film with Diksha Davakhar, his co-founder at production banner Davakhar Films. The company backs regional stories and aims for top-tier craft in camera work, sound, music and acting.

article_text:
For almost eight decades the artists’ model Louise Cansot, the subject of the novel winning France’s most prestigious literary prize this year, was one of Paris’s forgotten murder victims.

After her body was found near the Seine in September 1949, city police wrote off the young woman, immortalised as “the girl of 100 portraits”, as loose, libertine and – worse – an unmarried mother. They closed their investigation after just four months having made little effort to find her killer.

But long before the author Philippe Jaenada began researching his, Prix Goncourt-winning novel , L’ Inconnue du Quai de Javel (The Unknown Woman of the Quai de Javel) , another writer from the Breton village where Cansot was born had already spent decades researching her story.

Luc Corlouër might have felt aggrieved but in a rare show of literary solidarity, the two writers decided they would both publish books. As part of what he calls “the deal”, Corlouër handed Jaenada his notes.

“We agreed we would write our respective books, which are very different. And after all, the star was him, not me,” Corlouër told the Guardian. “By giving him the subject I knew he would make a really superb book. He is a great novelist.”

Cansot, nicknamed Lise, was born in Tréguier, on the Côtes-d’Armor in north-west France, the daughter of a shoe repairer. In 1937, aged 16, she left her family and moved to Paris where her beauty attracted the attention of the celebrated Montparnasse artists, who jostled to have her pose for them.

When war broke out and most of the artists fled south, Cansot remained in Paris working as a film extra, waiter and dancer at the Folies Bergère. She had a five-year-old daughter, Nathalie, whom she left with a nanny in the suburbs until she could raise the money for an apartment, but with the painters gone and no steady income, her situation became increasingly desperate.

On 7 September 1949, her body was found on the Quai du Javel, now known as the Quai André-Citroën, in the 15th arrondissement, south-west of the Eiffel Tower. Detectives initially identified four possible murderers but rapidly filed the case as unsolved.

Jaenada, the author of 17 novels, discovered the story while looking through old newspapers in the French National Library.

By then, Corlouër had already amassed maps, images, photos, paintings, documents, letters and newspaper cuttings on Cansot. His book, La Tragédie du plus beau modèle de Paris (The Tragedy of the Most Beautiful Paris Model) was finally published on 19 August – the same date as Jaenada’s novel – and is based on the documentary information about the case and the victim.

Corlouër says his interest in Cansot was piqued in 1981, when he met an elderly woman at the war memorial in Tréguier. “She told me one name was of a local girl, Annick Cansot, run over by a German truck during the war. When I said: ‘How terrible,’, she said even worse was that her older sister had been murdered in Paris.

“I decided I had to know about Louise Cansot and what happened to her, so I began researching, but my book was a failure. It was a novel about a murder investigation that did not identify the murderer. It was rejected by one publisher after another.

“I thought there was only one person capable of writing such a book: Philippe Jaenada, whom I had already met at a literary salon. Then one day he contacted me. He told me he was interested in the case but said he wouldn’t do anything without me.

“So, I entrusted him with my research. I gave it to him and he did the best investigation imaginable. He dissected all the information and found things I didn’t even think of.”

The original 300-page police report on Cansot’s murder concluded that she was a woman of “ill repute” and newspaper reports speculated that she was a sex worker, alcoholic or drug addict.

In his 530-page book, Jaenada gives a more sympathetic portrayal of the victim, and suggests the name of the man he believes strangled Cansot after inviting her to visit a flat she hoped to rent. His research included reading 74 out of the 75 novels by Georges Simenon featuring Inspector Maigret in 1940s Paris.

Corlouër said it was unsurprising the police had not made the same effort to find the killer back then.

“Lise was a very modern girl at least 50 years ahead of her time,” he said. “She dressed well, was intelligent and free in her choice of lovers. But when she was killed, what journalists and the police saw was a young woman who was a bit libertine, had a baby out of wedlock, had jobs they didn’t think were proper jobs and posed for painters. To them, she had brought what happened on herself.”

Corlouër said he and Jaenada had wanted to rehabilitate Cansot’s reputation after 77 years of slander. “In the police report it’s more or less written that she deserved it. And the defamation continued after her murder,” he said.

Corlouër also revealed how the authors traced Cansot’s daughter Nathalie, now 80, who was raised by another sister, Valentine.

“I don’t want to say too much because it would spoil the end of Philippe’s novel, but when we found her, the first thing she said was she didn’t want to hear a word about her mother and that Lise was a prostitute,” Corlouër said.

“She was raised by her aunt, who was very jealous of Lise and who for years told the girl her mother was disreputable. Nathalie was very surprised when Philippe and I told her this was not true, that her mother was an amazing woman.

“When she heard this, she did not cry. She’s tough like her mother, but she was amazed. So there is a kind of happy ending to this tragic story.”

Art Movements

Print Center and Women’s Studio Workshop Name New Leaders

Plus, SITE Santa Fe artists announced, awards for Lorna Simpson and Wolfgang Tillmans, and Penske Media partners with Amazon … because of course.

Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

Yukiko Yamagata to Helm NYC's Print Center

New York's Print Center, home to programs and exhibitions celebrating all the art that's pressed, proofed, and published, announced Yukiko Yamagata as its new executive director this week.

Her professional profile doesn't immediately scream “print nerd”: Yamagata most recently served as deputy director at Creative Time and previously worked at the Open Society Foundations, where she led a $15.8 million arts and culture fellowship program for socially engaged artists. But one of her earliest roles in the 1990s was as a senior curatorial assistant in the photo department at the Whitney Museum of American Art, and she is a current board member of Women Photograph, an organization focused on equitable practices in photojournalism and visual media.

Yamagata succeeds Judy Hecker , who announced her decision to step down earlier this year after a decade in the role, and is now executive director emerita.

Natalie Renganeschi to Lead Women's Studio Workshop

The Women's Studio Workshop in Rosendale, New York, dedicated to the printing arts as well as papermaking, bookbinding, photography, and more, has named Natalie Renganeschi as its fourth-ever executive director in the organization's 52-year history.

Renganeschi's career at WSW began in 2018, when she joined as a part-time employee while working as a high school art teacher. Now, she will oversee the nonprofit's major campus expansion, including the relaunch of its ceramics center.

“My path to leadership hasn’t been a traditional one, but it’s rooted in the ethos of WSW,” Renganeschi said in a statement. “Just as our mediums are steeped in process and the history of craft, working here is a sustained act of communal learning that allows for growth to come from below and within.”

Issue

One on One: Kimsooja on John Cage

JOHN CAGE ’s statement at the Paris Biennale, 1985. Courtesy Kimsooja Studio.

It is difficult for me to identify a single artist as the source of my artistic inspiration, yet if I had to name someone whose thinking greatly inspired my understanding of what art could be, it would be John Cage.

I first encountered Cage’s work at the Paris Biennale in 1985. I entered a white railway container expecting a sound installation; instead, I found an almost empty space and a statement, written in French along the corner of the floor: “ Que vous essayez de le faire ou pas, le son est entendu (Whether you try to make it or not, the sound is heard).” The encounter was immediate, revealing, and profound. I recognized Cage as a master—not because I wanted to follow his artistic language, but because his proposition articulated something fundamental: the world does not wait for the artist to make it exist; the artist simply creates the conditions through which we become attentive to it.

This realization resonated deeply with questions that I was exploring in my practice, and later became central to my approach of “non-doing” and “non-making.” These ideas do not mean an abstinence from action or making. Rather, they involve minimizing the artist’s intervention so that phenomena already present—light, sound, gravity, movement, reflection, breathing, and the passage of time—can reveal themselves. In this sense, the artist’s role is less about producing something new than creating a state of heightened perception.

article_text:
Lionsgate and Steven Paul ‘s SP Media are launching a new joint venture which will have the latter making a capital investment that will allow the former to continue its diversification of 3 Arts and other new businesses.

At the same time, the deal calls for SP Media to produce independent features films that Lionsgate will distribute. Lionsgate will have the majority stake in the joint venture, and will manage it.

Note, Paul is not becoming a minority investor in Lionsgate overall, rather a co-financier in the j.v. With Lionsgate, SP gains a distributor for its feature slate.

Related Stories

Lionsgate Stock Jumps On Report Of Takeover Offer By Legendary

'La La Land' Stage Musical Taps Film's Choreographer & Costume Designer; 59 Studio Aboard As Production Designer

The news comes at an interesting time with Legendary in due diligence with Lionsgate after sending the corporation a takeover offer last Tuesday. Sources tell Deadline that no formal process is underway for Lionsgate to accept acquisition offers; meaning no bankers have been hired.

Watch on Deadline

Paul is the chairman, founder and CEO of Crystal Sky Pictures and SP Media Group, and has shepherded such franchises as Baby Geniuses , as well as Ghost Rider and Ghost Rider 2: Spirit of Vengeance , starring Nicolas Cage, Ghost in the Shell , starring Scarlett Johansson, and the Lionsgate-distributed Rambo: Last Blood .

SP Media Group President & COO Scott Karol and Paul, are special advisors to Donald Trump Hollywood Ambassador Jon Voight, and have been working with federal lawmakers and industry groups on bipartisan legislation aimed at creating a U.S. film and TV tax credit and curbing runaway production.

In the summer of 2024, when David Ellison’s Skydance was pursuing Paramount, Paul spearheaded a group of investors that included John Paul DeJoria, the billionaire co-founder of Patron tequila and Paul Mitchell hair care products, to make a $2.25 billion offer for National Amusements Inc., the Redstone family holding company that owned 77% of Paramount’s voting stock.

“Steven is a savvy & experienced entrepreneur who has a longstanding relationship with our studio, and I’m pleased to partner with him across multiple touchpoints of our business,” said Lionsgate CEO Jon Feltheimer. “He recognizes the unique and valuable assets that we have built and his investment will help drive the continued growth of these businesses.”

“Lionsgate is one of the most dynamic and entrepreneurial content studios in the media space today,” said Paul. “I’m delighted to build on my longstanding relationship with Jon Feltheimer and the Lionsgate leadership team as we grow our businesses together in an industry environment filled with opportunity.”

The joint venture deal with SP Media was negotiated for Lionsgate by COO Brian Goldsmith, EVP & General Counsel Bruce Tobey, and Senior VP Corporate Development Suzy Felfeli and for SP Media by Karol. Moelis served as financial advisor to Lionsgate and Lazard served as financial advisor to SP Media. Paul Hastings LLP represented SP Media on the deal.

Jill Goldsmith contributed to this piece.

Opinion

I’m an Epstein Survivor. MoMA Must Drop Leon Black.

Institutions must reckon with the possibility that their prestige can be used to legitimize people whose conduct warrants serious investigations.

House Oversight Committee (photo illustration Valentina Di Liscia/

Hyperallergic )

For more than two decades, one question has followed me since I was abused by Jeffrey Epstein: “Why me?”

In trying to understand what happened, I have come to recognize that the answer lies not only in the manipulation I endured, but also in the institutions and social structures that helped make that manipulation possible.

Leon Black’s board position at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) is one of the starkest examples of institutional ignorance — a head-in-the-sand, look-the-other-way mentality that will inevitably give abuse of power a dark corner to grow and fester in.

article_text:
Times change, the arc of the moral universe bends towards justice, and yet one thing that has remained true for as long as I’ve been alive is that prejudice, bigotry, and explicit displays of racism have always been openly permissible in America — so long as they’ve been targeted at Arabs and/or Muslims. That sad and immutable fact was on full display throughout Zohran Mamdani’s mayoral campaign last year, and the say the quiet part out loud reaction to Abdul El-Sayed’s current senate race has somehow managed to be even worse on both sides of the aisle (Democrats lament that he “doesn’t share our values,” while Republicans straight up just call the guy a jihadist). But anyone old enough to remember 9/11 knows that it didn’t start with the likes of Vicky Paladino , just as I assume that anyone old enough to remember the assassination of Alex Odeh knows that it didn’t start with 9/11.

The sole fatality of a bomb that had been planted at the California office where he served as the West Coast Regional Director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC), Alexander Michel Odeh was murdered on the morning of October 11, 1985, leaving behind his wife Norma and their three young daughters Helena, Samya, and Susan. To this day, his slaughter remains “unsolved.” And yet, as Jason Osder and William Youmans’ scattered but vital documentary “ Who Killed Alex Odeh? ” makes clear soon after it begins, there’s little doubt as to who was behind the killing.

Indeed, the film establishes that the case was effectively solved within days of the attack, and that all three of the primary suspects — all members of a right-wing terrorist group known as the Jewish Defense League — were only allowed to flee to Israel because powerful forces within the American political system preferred for them to get away with it. And to get away with it. And to get away with it. More than 40 years later, no efforts have been made to prosecute or extradite the presumptive murderers. One of them has even moved back to the United States.

And so, despite affecting the aesthetic and tropes of the true-crime format, “Who Killed Alex Odeh?” directly contradicts the expectations of its supposed genre. Instead of establishing a vast mystery for their movie to explore, Osder and Youmans — one of them Jewish, the other a Palestinian-American — give shape to the galling absence of one. Stunted and searching by design, their film unpacks the sociopolitical context of Odeh’s killing in order to illustrate how the easily Google-able question posed by its title could possibly remain “unanswered” for so long, and even partakes in some light subterfuge as part of an effort to pin down the culprits on camera.

What the documentary finds, or at least calls new attention towards, is alternately eye-opening, obvious, and eye-opening for its obviousness. First and foremost, Osder and Youmans use Odeh’s murder as a lens through which to examine the militarization of Jewish extremism at home and abroad (with an emphasis on the emergence of ultra-nationalist JDL founder Meir Kahane). Propelled by archival footage, the film has little room for personal reflection, but implicit in its focus is the willfully short-sighted extent to which “terrorism” has long been framed as an exclusively Muslim practice; Osder suggests in the press notes, but not the documentary itself, that American Jews are seldom taught about the more violent expressions of Zionism, an implication supported by my own memories of going to Hebrew School at a conservative New England synagogue.

“Who Killed Alex Odeh?” also examines how the tacit permission of such violence is what also allows it to ferment. That Israel welcomed Odeh’s alleged killers back to the holy land, and that President Reagan refused to recognize the severity of the hate crime they had committed against a fellow American on American soil (he never so much as sent a letter of condolence to Odeh’s widow), sent a clear and enduring message that the world’s most powerful governments were okay with the spilling of Palestinian blood. It’s since been alleged that Mossad and the U.S. State Department combined to shut down the murder investigation.

In the most harrowing sequence of a film that has little use for suspense, Israeli investigative journalist David Sheen disguises himself as an ultra-Orthodox Jew and meets one of the alleged killers while wearing a hidden camera — Baruch Ben-Yosef’s outspoken prejudices seem inextricable from his comfortable position as a pillar of his community. Later, when Osder lures him into a sit-down interview under false pretenses, Ben-Yosef excuses himself from the conversation when Odeh’s name is mentioned, his irritation softened (and made even more upsetting) by the “this again?” attitude of someone who seems to believe that no one could possibly still give a shit about the 1985 murder of a single Palestinian expat.

Somewhat diminished in the film’s erratic attempts to contextualize this ever-metastasizing sickness is Odeh himself. Born in Palestine but displaced to Egypt as a child because of the 1967 Arab-Israeli War, the righteous but mild-mannered Odeh dedicated his adult life to combating discrimination against his people in America. Home video footage and old clips from his television panel appearances paint Odeh as more of an egghead than a firebrand. He worked to make in-roads with the local Jewish community, and didn’t have much of a public profile aside from an occasional appearance on “Newsline.” During his final appearance on the show, he debated a member of the JDL.

Osder and Youmans also interview members of Odeh’s immediate family, whose “what is there to say besides the obvious?” has already been internalized by the rest of the documentary. A different and possibly more rewarding film might have done more to investigate the pain of living in a country that has all but signed off on the hate-based murder of your husband or father, but “Who Killed Alex Odeh?” has little patience for investigations. The only thing more obvious than the identity of Odeh’s murderers is the continued lack of political will to hold them accountable. And a country that lacks the political will to address the slaughter of one Palestinian is a country that lacks the political will to address the slaughter of Palestine itself.

Grade: B

“Who Killed Alex Odeh?” is now playing in theaters.

article_text:
自画像 47KMの死

劇場公開日： 2026年11月12日

解説・あらすじ

中国湖北省の農村に通い続け、村の人々と自身の変化を記録してきたジャン・モンチーの「自画像 47KM」シリーズ第5作。村と彼女を結ぶ存在だった祖父の死をきっかけに、監督が村を覆う無数の死と向き合った記録となった。 2010年、大学を出たばかりのジャン・モンチー監督は、老人たちへのインタビューのため父の故郷である湖北省の村「47KM村」を訪れ、以来毎年通い続けてきた。だが、村と自分をつないでいた祖父が亡くなり、彼女は村にとどまる意義を見失う。死とはどういうものなのか。監督は老人たちにカメラの前で語ってもらう。農薬を飲んで自ら命を絶った老人、批判闘争でつるし上げられて死んだ人々。穏やかに見えた日常は、実は無数の死に囲まれていた。それでも監督は、村の若者たちに希望を見いだそうとする。 シリーズは第1作「自画像 47KM」から第10作「自画像 47KM 2020」まで10本を数え、監督は2020年から村に家を建てて暮らしている。日本初上映となる本作は、全10本をまとめて上映する「ジャン・モンチー監督 47KMシリーズ特集上映」（2026年11月7～20日＝ポレポレ東中野）で公開。

監督

Art Review

A Felix Gonzalez-Torres Exhibition Forgets What He Was Fighting For

“Sweet Revenge” at the Reina Sofía gives the impression of a showcase of a second-generation Minimalist artist, emphasizing form over anything else.

Hyperallergic )

MADRID — The long-awaited exhibition Felix Gonzalez-Torres: Sweet Revenge at the Museo Reina Sofía opens with an emphasis on Madrid’s role in the artist's life. Gonzalez-Torres briefly lived here as a Cuban child refugee in 1971 before moving on to Puerto Rico and New York. While this marks his first large-scale solo exhibition in the Spanish capital, it follows a landmark show at the Centro Galego de Arte Contemporánea in Santiago de Compostela in 1995, just before his death from AIDS-related complications; a 2000 group show ( No es sólo lo que ves: Pervirtiendo el Minimalismo) at the Reina Sofía itself; and a 2021 exhibition at the Museu d’Art Contemporani de Barcelona framed by the COVID-19 pandemic. By centering his brief history as a refugee, the present exhibition challenges our traditional understanding of Gonzalez-Torres's trajectory. Why, though, are many of his most politically charged works missing?

The exhibition unfolds across seven galleries on the first floor of the Sabatini Building, featuring more than 50 works by Gonzalez-Torres: his iconic candy spills, text portraits, puzzles, beaded curtains, paper stacks, and photographs, alongside quotes by the artist printed on the gallery walls. Strikingly, there is no chronological framework. The exhibition was curated by artist Alejandro Cesarco and Nancy Spector, the former Guggenheim artistic director and chief curator who organized Gonzalez-Torres's definitive 1995 retrospective in New York. They drew inspiration for the show's title and central theme from the blue candy spill “‘ Untitled’ (Revenge) ” (1991), a work the artist created after returning to Madrid as an adult. He would later reflect on the personal significance of the visit: “I returned to Madrid nearly twenty years later — sweet revenge.” According to a wall text, being sent to Madrid as a child refugee “was a traumatic experience, one that heavily informed his preoccupations with memory and repetition.”

Felix Gonzalez-Torres: Sweet Revenge with "'Untitled' (Revenge)" (1991) (photo Roberto Ruiz, courtesy Museo Reina Sofía)

Adopting “Sweet Revenge” as their operational framework, the curators highlight the ambiguity and complexity of Gonzalez-Torres’s works, which often oscillate between aesthetic beauty and critical engagement. They present a parallel text titled "Methodology" in the entrance hall, outlining the principles, instructions, and responsibilities that guide the exhibition. This text explains the logistics behind the replenishable candy piles, paper stacks, and alterable text portraits, detailing how they are to be presented and expanded upon. Ultimately, the curators seem to focus more on the mechanics of Gonzalez-Torres's works than on what he was trying to say.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 英籍摩洛哥摄影师哈桑·哈贾吉（Hassan Hajjaj）携大约四十幅音量开足的肖像作品进驻巴黎爱乐音乐厅：这些都是他专属的摇滚巨星，从麦当娜到马里二人组阿马杜与玛丽亚姆（Amadou & Mariam）。L’article Hassan Hajjaj, the Eye That Grooves est apparu en premier sur Blind…
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "为阿马杜与玛丽亚姆拍摄的那次写真依然是他最喜欢的经历之一。作为巴马科这个双人组合的狂热拥趸，哈桑·哈贾吉为他们打造了一张串烧了根纳瓦（Gnawa）音乐和巴西卡波耶拉（capoeira）的播放列表，那种质感极其厚重、宛如能用双手握住的音乐；当拍摄接近尾声时，反倒是音乐人们主动向他索要这份曲目单。他一直都是这样工作的：镜头在手，音乐在耳。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他于1961年出生于摩洛哥西北海岸的渔镇拉腊什，在形形色色的摄影师身边长大。在街道上和沙滩上，照片被定格，一张纸质凭据在人们手中传递，几天后冲印好的照片便会现身。在照相馆里，凳子和背景幕布随时待命，他与穿着节日盛装的家人一同前去拍摄肖像，每隔两年，这张照片就会寄给远在伦敦工作的父亲。1973年，这个十三岁的男孩也跟随前往，一头扎进1970年代末期的种族紧张局势之中，游走于牙买加音响系统（sound systems）与“抗击种族主义摇滚”（Rock Against Racism）之间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览策展人伊内丝·热夫鲁瓦（Inès Geoffroy）总结道：“音乐创造了纽带与联系”；对于这个根基离析的男孩来说，音乐将成为一种共同的语言，并且已经成为了一种武器。1984年，哈桑·哈贾吉在科芬园尼尔街（Neal Street）开设了“真正的艺术人们”（Real Artistic People）店：一家DIY服装店（充满创意的凑合、部分由手工制作、部分则是激进的废物利用），地下室里堆满了可供翻找的黑胶唱片。他在T恤上印上“香奈儿5号属于古驰”（Chanel No. 5 for Gucci），将薇薇安·韦斯特伍德（Vivienne Westwood）的风格与纽约嘻哈音乐拼接在一起，还将恶搞标签缝在牛仔夹克的背面。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这家店后来成了音乐家、画家、摄影师和诗人们的巢穴，也就是哈桑·哈贾吉后来所称的他的“大学”。《Yo! MTV Raps》的传奇主持人法布5·弗雷迪（Fab 5 Freddy）有一天推门而入，当场便看懂了他的计划：“嘻哈时尚与街头风格中摩洛哥、阿拉伯、穆斯林的这一面，”这位艺术家在接受《Blind》采访时回忆道。他拍摄的方式也源于同源之处。他亲自为拍摄对象挑选服装：几何印花的杰拉巴长袍（djellabas）、点缀着被恶搞徽标的传统尖头皮鞋（babouches）、酸糖果色调的卡夫坦长袍（kaftans）、波尔卡圆点或山寨奢侈品徽章的面纱，整个场景则以织造而成的多色塑料为背景进行搭建。", A devotee of the Bamako duo, Hassan Hajjaj built them a playlist of Gnawa and Brazilian capoeira, something earthy enough to hold in your hands; when the shoot wound down, the musicians were the ones asking him for the tracklist. He has always worked like this: lens in hand, music in the ear."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Born in 1961 in Larache, a fishing town on Morocco’s northwest coast, he grows up among photographers of every stripe. On the street and the sand, the picture is taken, a paper slip changes hands, and the print turns up a few days later. In the studio, stool and backdrop at the ready, he comes with the family in their Sunday best to sit for the portrait posted, every two years, to the father who has left to work in London. The boy follows in 1973, at thirteen, straight into the racial tensions of the late 1970s, somewhere between the Jamaican sound systems and Rock Against Racism."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Music creates bonds and connections,” sums up Inès Geoffroy, the exhibition’s curator; for this uprooted boy it will be a shared tongue, and already a weapon. In 1984, Hassan Hajjaj opens Real Artistic People on Neal Street, Covent Garden: a do-it-yourself clothing shop (creative make-do, part handmade craft, part militant recycling) with a basement of vinyl to rummage through. He prints “Chanel No. 5 for Gucci” on T-shirts, splices Vivienne Westwood into New York hip-hop, stitches spoof labels onto the backs of denim jackets."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The shop turns into a den for musicians, painters, photographers and poets, what Hassan Hajjaj will later call his “university.” Fab 5 Freddy, the cult host of Yo! article_text:
The session with Amadou & Mariam stays among his favorites. A devotee of the Bamako duo, Hassan Hajjaj built them a playlist of Gnawa and Brazilian capoeira, something earthy enough to hold in your hands; when the shoot wound down, the musicians were the ones asking him for the tracklist. He has always worked like this: lens in hand, music in the ear.

Born in 1961 in Larache, a fishing town on Morocco’s northwest coast, he grows up among photographers of every stripe. On the street and the sand, the picture is taken, a paper slip changes hands, and the print turns up a few days later. In the studio, stool and backdrop at the ready, he comes with the family in their Sunday best to sit for the portrait posted, every two years, to the father who has left to work in London. The boy follows in 1973, at thirteen, straight into the racial tensions of the late 1970s, somewhere between the Jamaican sound systems and Rock Against Racism.

“Music creates bonds and connections,” sums up Inès Geoffroy, the exhibition’s curator; for this uprooted boy it will be a shared tongue, and already a weapon. In 1984, Hassan Hajjaj opens Real Artistic People on Neal Street, Covent Garden: a do-it-yourself clothing shop (creative make-do, part handmade craft, part militant recycling) with a basement of vinyl to rummage through. He prints “Chanel No. 5 for Gucci” on T-shirts, splices Vivienne Westwood into New York hip-hop, stitches spoof labels onto the backs of denim jackets.

The shop turns into a den for musicians, painters, photographers and poets, what Hassan Hajjaj will later call his “university.” Fab 5 Freddy, the cult host of Yo! MTV Raps , pushes through the door one day and reads his project on sight: “the Moroccan, Arab, Muslim side of hip-hop fashion and street style,” the artist recalled to Blind. The way he shoots comes from the same place. He dresses his subjects himself: djellabas in geometric print, babouches trimmed with hijacked logos, kaftans the color of sour sweets, veils in polka dots or counterfeit luxury crests, the whole thing staged against backdrops of woven, multicolored plastic.

“He really had this approach, a bit like making a great mix: sampling, collecting motifs, formats, colors,” Inès Geoffroy observes, “a world where design and music stand on the same level.” The Malian masters Seydou Keïta and Malick Sidibé, who invented the modern African studio portrait, preside over every frame; Hassan Hajjaj claims them as forefathers, then tilts their legacy toward a language all his own: hybrid, festive, gloriously cobbled together.

The photographer helps himself to the European cliché of the rock star, leather jacket, Ray-Bans, electric guitar, and hands the crown to his own instead. Madonna makes the case: shot in Marrakech for her sixtieth birthday, she sits in babouches sewn from rice sacks, a mock-Gucci print, a would-be Louis Vuitton hat, every piece made by Hassan Hajjaj. Veiled, hidden behind her shades, she turns unrecognizable, then leaves for the airport without changing a thing.

Lee Scratch Perry, the high priest of Jamaican dub, turns up as a silent watcher on set. The photographer slides a pair of plastic shoes his way; the musician pulls them on at once and, that same night, takes the stage in the full getup. Others file past the lens too: Keziah Jones, Cardi B, then Alicia Keys and her husband, the producer Swizz Beatz, who collect his work. The show’s poster goes to Billie Eilish: in 2019, on a Vogue shoot in Los Angeles, Hassan Hajjaj talks the singer, barely eighteen and chaperoned by her mother, into his own designs. “I’ve met so many incredible people, who are my real rock stars,” he told Blind, “what they do, they have it in their blood.”

The frames he builds himself, worked like sculpture. “What really makes the signature is framing the photos with tin cans, salvaged or made by his own hand,” notes Marion Challier, curator; “Hassan Hajjaj is deeply attached to salvage as a way of life.” Harissa, tomato, green tea, their logos curling into Arabic, run around the edge of every portrait. Each print is dated twice over, Gregorian and Hijri: a quiet reminder that time itself keeps different counts from one shore to the next.

At the Philharmonie as in his life, Gnawa runs through everything. After twelve years of London’s electronic nights, hungry for something to feed the soul, Hassan Hajjaj goes back to the sound of this brotherhood of healer-musicians, in Marrakech, in the early 1990s. The exhibition’s own soundtrack may come from Acid Arab, electronica braided into Arab tradition over a bed of acid house, yet it is two Gnawa masters, Ba Bohot and Khadija Lgnawia, who hold pride of place. A tribute to a culture from which he drew, he confides, “something that touched my spirit, my heart, my frequencies.”

“Hassan Hajjaj, My Rock Stars” is on view at the Musée de la musique – Philharmonie de Paris through April 25, 2027.
